title: Conjecture 2
context_text: A majority colouring of a digraph is an assignment of colours to the vertices such that, for every vertex $v$, at most half of the out-neighbours of $v$ receive the same colour as $v$ (colourings need not be proper; $\deg^+(v)$ is the out-degree); a majority $k$-colouring uses at most $k$ colours. Whether a bounded number of colours always suffices was asked on MathOverflow, and Ilya Bogdanov proved it for tournaments. The authors prove that every digraph has a majority $4$-colouring (partition the arcs into two acyclic digraphs, 2-colour each greedily along a topological order, and take the product colouring). They conjecture that $3$ colours suffice, which would be best possible: in an odd directed cycle every out-degree is $1$, so a majority colouring is a proper colouring and needs $3$ colours, and circulant digraphs with $N^+(v_i)=\{v_{i+1},\dots,v_{i+k}\}$ for odd $k$ and prime $n\gg k$ show that large out-degree does not help. They prove the conjecture for digraphs of minimum out-degree greater than $72\log(3n)$, and for digraphs of minimum out-degree at least $1200$ and maximum in-degree at most $\exp(\delta/72)/12\delta$ ($\delta$ the minimum out-degree).

title: Conjecture 9
statement_text: For $k \geq 2$, every digraph has a vertex $(k+1)$-colouring such that for each vertex $v$, at most $\frac{1}{k}\deg^+(v)$ out-neighbours of $v$ receive the same colour as $v$.
context_text: A majority colouring of a digraph is an assignment of colours to the vertices such that, for every vertex $v$, at most half of the out-neighbours of $v$ receive the same colour as $v$ (colourings need not be proper; $\deg^+(v)$ is the out-degree); a majority $k$-colouring uses at most $k$ colours. Whether a bounded number of colours always suffices was asked on MathOverflow, and Ilya Bogdanov proved it for tournaments. The authors prove that every digraph has a majority $4$-colouring (partition the arcs into two acyclic digraphs, 2-colour each greedily along a topological order, and take the product colouring). The same proof generalises to give $k^2$ colours with at most $\frac1k\deg^+(v)$ same-coloured out-neighbours, and it is open whether $O(k)$ colours suffice. The case $k=2$ of the conjecture is the conjecture that every digraph has a majority 3-colouring. It would be best possible: the $k$-th power of a directed $n$-cycle (each vertex pointing to the next $k$ vertices) with $n\ge2k+3$ and $n\not\equiv0\pmod{k+1}$ has no $(k+1)$-colouring in which every vertex has fewer than one out-neighbour of its colour. For undirected graphs, Lovász proved that every graph has a $k$-colouring in which every vertex $v$ has at most $\frac1k\deg(v)$ neighbours of its colour.

title: Open Problem 1
statement_text: Is there a constant $\beta < 1$ for which every digraph has a 3-colouring such that for every vertex $v$, at most $\beta \deg^+(v)$ out-neighbours receive the same colour as $v$?
context_text: A majority colouring of a digraph is an assignment of colours to the vertices such that, for every vertex $v$, at most half of the out-neighbours of $v$ receive the same colour as $v$ (colourings need not be proper; $\deg^+(v)$ is the out-degree); a majority $k$-colouring uses at most $k$ colours. Whether a bounded number of colours always suffices was asked on MathOverflow, and Ilya Bogdanov proved it for tournaments. The authors prove that every digraph has a majority $4$-colouring (partition the arcs into two acyclic digraphs, 2-colour each greedily along a topological order, and take the product colouring). The case $\beta=\frac12$ is the authors' conjecture that every digraph has a majority 3-colouring, which they prove under extra degree assumptions: minimum out-degree greater than $72\log(3n)$, or minimum out-degree $\delta\ge1200$ and maximum in-degree at most $\exp(\delta/72)/12\delta$. For Eulerian digraphs (in-degree equal to out-degree at every vertex), an argument of Lovász gives a 3-colouring in which each vertex $v$ has at most $\frac23\deg(v)$ in- or out-neighbours of its colour, proving a special case of this question.

title: Open Problem 2
statement_text: Does every tournament have a majority 3-colouring?
context_text: A majority colouring of a digraph is an assignment of colours to the vertices such that, for every vertex $v$, at most half of the out-neighbours of $v$ receive the same colour as $v$ (colourings need not be proper; $\deg^+(v)$ is the out-degree); a majority $k$-colouring uses at most $k$ colours. Whether a bounded number of colours always suffices was asked on MathOverflow, and Ilya Bogdanov proved it for tournaments. The authors prove that every digraph has a majority $4$-colouring (partition the arcs into two acyclic digraphs, 2-colour each greedily along a topological order, and take the product colouring). Bogdanov's bound for tournaments (orientations of complete graphs) uses a bounded number of colours, but it is open whether $3$ colours always suffice; this is a special case of the authors' conjecture that every digraph has a majority 3-colouring.

title: Open Problem 3
statement_text: Does every Eulerian digraph have a majority 3-colouring?
context_text: A majority colouring of a digraph is an assignment of colours to the vertices such that, for every vertex $v$, at most half of the out-neighbours of $v$ receive the same colour as $v$ (colourings need not be proper; $\deg^+(v)$ is the out-degree); a majority $k$-colouring uses at most $k$ colours. Whether a bounded number of colours always suffices was asked on MathOverflow, and Ilya Bogdanov proved it for tournaments. The authors prove that every digraph has a majority $4$-colouring (partition the arcs into two acyclic digraphs, 2-colour each greedily along a topological order, and take the product colouring). An Eulerian digraph is one in which every vertex $v$ has in-degree equal to its out-degree, say $\deg(v)$. By Lovász's result that every undirected graph has a $k$-colouring in which each vertex $v$ has at most $\frac1k\deg(v)$ neighbours of its colour, applied to the underlying graph with $k=4$, every Eulerian digraph has a majority 4-colouring, and an analogous argument gives a 3-colouring in which each vertex has at most $\frac23\deg(v)$ in- or out-neighbours of its colour. Whether a majority 3-colouring always exists is open.

title: Open Problem 4
statement_text: Does every digraph in which every vertex has in-degree and out-degree $k$ have a majority 3-colouring?
context_text: A variant of Theorem 4 (using the Lovász Local Lemma) proves this for $k \geq 144$; the case of small $k$ is open.

title: Open Problem 5
statement_text: Is there a characterisation of digraphs that have a majority 2-colouring, or a polynomial-time algorithm to recognise such digraphs?
context_text: A majority colouring of a digraph is an assignment of colours to the vertices such that, for every vertex $v$, at most half of the out-neighbours of $v$ receive the same colour as $v$ (colourings need not be proper; $\deg^+(v)$ is the out-degree); a majority $k$-colouring uses at most $k$ colours. Whether a bounded number of colours always suffices was asked on MathOverflow, and Ilya Bogdanov proved it for tournaments. The authors prove that every digraph has a majority $4$-colouring (partition the arcs into two acyclic digraphs, 2-colour each greedily along a topological order, and take the product colouring). Not every digraph has a majority 2-colouring (an odd directed cycle does not), and majority 2-colourability is not closed under taking induced subdigraphs: the digraph with vertices $a,b,c,d$ and arcs $ab,bc,ca,cd$ has the majority 2-colouring giving colour $1$ to $a,c$ and colour $2$ to $b,d$, but its induced subdigraph on $\{a,b,c\}$ is a directed triangle, which has none. Every acyclic digraph has a majority 2-colouring (colour greedily in reverse topological order).

title: Open Problem 6
statement_text: Does every digraph have an $O(k)$-colouring such that for each vertex $v$, at most $\frac{1}{k}\deg^+(v)$ out-neighbours receive the same colour as $v$ (for all $k \geq 2$)?
context_text: The current upper bound from the proof of Theorem 1 is $k^2$ colours for the generalised Conjecture 9; it is explicitly noted as open whether $O(k)$ colours suffice.

title: Open Problem 7
statement_text: A digraph $G$ is majority $c$-choosable if for every assignment of a set $L(v)$ of integers to each vertex $v\in V(G)$ with $|L(v)| \geq c$ for each vertex $v$, there is a majority colouring of $G$ with each vertex $v$ coloured from $L(v)$. Is every digraph majority $c$-choosable for some constant $c$?
context_text: A majority colouring of a digraph is an assignment of colours to the vertices such that, for every vertex $v$, at most half of the out-neighbours of $v$ receive the same colour as $v$ (colourings need not be proper; $\deg^+(v)$ is the out-degree); a majority $k$-colouring uses at most $k$ colours. Whether a bounded number of colours always suffices was asked on MathOverflow, and Ilya Bogdanov proved it for tournaments. The authors prove that every digraph has a majority $4$-colouring (partition the arcs into two acyclic digraphs, 2-colour each greedily along a topological order, and take the product colouring). The proof of the 4-colour result shows that acyclic digraphs are majority 2-choosable, and the authors' probabilistic results (a majority 3-colouring exists when the minimum out-degree exceeds $72\log(3n)$, or when the minimum out-degree $\delta$ is at least $1200$ and the maximum in-degree at most $\exp(\delta/72)/12\delta$) extend to the choosability setting.

title: Open Problem 8
statement_text: Call a set $T$ of vertices of a digraph $G$ stable if for each vertex $v\in T$, at most half the out-neighbours of $v$ are also in $T$. Let $S(G)$ be the set of all stable sets of $G$ and $S(G,v)$ the stable sets containing $v$. A fractional majority colouring assigns each $T \in S(G)$ a weight $x_T \geq 0$ such that $\sum_{T \in S(G,v)} x_T \geq 1$ for each vertex $v$. What is the minimum $k$ such that every digraph $G$ has a fractional majority colouring with $\sum_{T \in S(G)} x_T \leq k$? Perhaps $k < 3$.
context_text: A majority colouring of a digraph is an assignment of colours to the vertices such that, for every vertex $v$, at most half of the out-neighbours of $v$ receive the same colour as $v$ (colourings need not be proper; $\deg^+(v)$ is the out-degree); a majority $k$-colouring uses at most $k$ colours. Whether a bounded number of colours always suffices was asked on MathOverflow, and Ilya Bogdanov proved it for tournaments. The authors prove that every digraph has a majority $4$-colouring (partition the arcs into two acyclic digraphs, 2-colour each greedily along a topological order, and take the product colouring). A majority colouring is exactly a partition of the vertex set into stable sets in the above sense (not the usual independent sets), so a fractional majority colouring is the natural LP relaxation, and the answer is at most $4$ by the authors' theorem. They also show that every digraph with minimum out-degree at least $22$ has a stable set with at least a third of the vertices, and that large minimum out-degree forces stable sets of nearly half the vertices. The guess $k<3$ would be a fractional analogue of the conjecture that every digraph has a majority 3-colouring.
notes: The 'perhaps $k < 3$' is an informal conjectural remark embedded within the open problem statement.
